Instructions for Coding Agents

Source: AGENTS.md

Required Windows preflight check

On Windows, at the beginning of the first task, before making changes or running development, build, or test workflows, compare the current environment with the last successful preflight check stored in _dev/windows-preflight.json relative to the repository root. This is a local cache: do not commit it or include it in the built package (_dev is already excluded from both).

  • Always obtain the active R installation’s R.version.string and R.home() from the R installation actually used by the current session or task. Do not infer them from another installed R executable.
  • Obtain a system ID consisting of the computer name and the Windows version, including its build and update revision. For example, use $env:COMPUTERNAME and DisplayVersion, CurrentBuildNumber, and UBR from HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion in PowerShell.
  • Read the cache and compare rVersion, rHome, and systemId with these current values. If all values match and status is passed, reuse the successful result and skip the full Rtools compatibility and compilation checks. Do not repeat those checks merely because a new task or session starts.
  • Run the full check below only if the cache is missing, unreadable, incomplete, or not marked passed, or if the R version, R installation path, or system ID has changed. A changed R version always requires a new full check.
  • If the current environment cannot be identified, stop and explain what could not be verified; do not reuse an unverifiable cached result.

For a required full check:

  • Identify the R installation actually used by the current session or task. Obtain its full version from R.version.string and its installation path from R.home() using that same R installation. Do not infer the active version from another installed R executable.
  • Determine the Rtools release required for that R version using the official Rtools compatibility guidance. Do not assume that the newest installed Rtools release is compatible.
  • Verify that the matching Rtools installation is usable by that R session, including its build tools and C/C++ compilers. Use a toolchain diagnostic that verifies compilation with the active R installation; finding an installation directory alone is not sufficient.
  • If matching Rtools is missing, incompatible, or unusable, stop the task and notify the user. The message must state the active R version and installation path, the expected Rtools release, and the reason the check failed. Ask the user to install or configure the matching Rtools and make it accessible to the active R installation before work resumes.
  • If compatibility or usability cannot be established, stop and explain what could not be verified rather than proceeding with an unverified toolchain.

After the full check succeeds, create _dev if needed and write the JSON cache with status = "passed", rVersion, rHome, systemId, the verified rtoolsRelease, rtoolsHome, and checkedAt (an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp). Use the values actually verified, and replace the cache only after all required checks succeed. On failure, invalidate any existing successful cache by setting status = "failed"; never record an unsuccessful or unverified check as passed. If saving the cache fails, report that limitation; the next task must perform the full check again. If a later build reveals a toolchain failure, invalidate the cache so that the next task checks the toolchain again.

Task-specific guidance

Read and follow the applicable instruction files before starting work. If a task spans multiple categories, apply all relevant files:

  • Bug fixing or refactoring: Read .github/agents/rpact_bugfix_refactor.agent.md.
  • General development: Read .github/agents/rpact_general.agent.md.
  • Creating unit tests or improving test coverage: Read .github/agents/rpact_testcoverage.agent.md and follow the test location requirements below.
  • Tasks involving GitHub: Read .github/agents/rpact_github.agent.md.

Required error handling in R code

All errors raised explicitly by rpact code under R/ must use the appropriate error helper from R/f_error_handling.R. Direct calls to stop() (including base::stop(), rethrowing caught conditions, and calls hidden behind aliases or new wrappers) are prohibited. The only permitted direct call is the existing stop(condition) in .stopWithError() in R/f_error_handling.R; keep this as the single central error-signalling point. Existing violations elsewhere are not examples to follow.

Before adding or changing an error path, read R/f_error_handling.R and inspect comparable calls in the package, especially in R/f_core_assertions.R and R/class_design_optimal.R. Reuse a suitable existing assertion when it already performs the required validation and supplies the appropriate error metadata. Otherwise, call the most specific helper below rather than calling .stopWithError() or .createCondition() directly.

Helper Use for
stopMissingArgument() A required argument is absent.
stopArgumentUnknown() An unknown or unsupported argument name.
stopIllegalArgument() An invalid argument type, value, or option not covered by a more specific helper.
stopArgumentOutOfRange() An argument value outside its allowed bounds.
stopArgumentLengthOutOfBounds() An argument with an invalid length.
stopIndexOutOfBounds() An invalid index.
stopConflictingArguments() Mutually incompatible arguments or parameterizations.
stopIncompleteArguments() A partially supplied set of arguments requiring companion parameters.
stopIllegalDataInput() Invalid input data or inconsistent dataset contents.
stopRuntimeIssue() An internal, execution, or computational failure rather than invalid user input.

Supply structured diagnostic information

A message alone is insufficient for new or revised error calls. These helpers feed the configurable condition factories (rpact.error.factory.*) and provide consistent exception prefixes, codes, categories, and condition classes. Supply the diagnostic information as named helper arguments, not just as text in the message:

  • Always specify functionName: the function or method whose validation or operation failed. In a reusable assertion, propagate the caller’s function name when its interface supports this; otherwise use the assertion’s name, following comparable existing calls.
  • For argument or data errors, specify parameter (the relevant name or names) and value (the actual offending value). Preserve the value’s R type rather than converting it to display text. Do not evaluate a missing argument just to populate value; omit it or use NULL when no value exists.
  • Specify constraint to describe the violated requirement. For dependent or conflicting inputs, also supply relatedParameter and relatedValue.
  • Use the helper’s specific fields when applicable: lowerBound and upperBound for ranges or indices; expectedLength and actualLength for lengths; index for invalid indexing; missingParameters and definedParameters for incomplete argument sets. Describe open or closed bounds in constraint as well.
  • Supply a stable, meaningful diagnosticId for the failure rule. Reuse an existing ID for the same rule; follow the existing dotted naming convention (for example, validation.values_outside_interval). Do not put runtime values, translated messages, or line numbers in an ID, or reuse an unrelated ID merely because the helper is the same.
  • Add context = list(...) with named entries for useful additional facts not covered by the dedicated fields, such as the affected stage, object position, allowed choices, or computational operation. For runtime failures without an offending argument, supply the relevant operational context. Include only information available at the failure site; do not invent values or fill irrelevant fields with placeholders.
  • Use only formal metadata arguments supported by the chosen helper. Its ... arguments are concatenated into the message by .getErrorMessage(); arbitrary named entries in ... do not become structured metadata. Put additional diagnostic fields in the named context list.

Keep the message clear and actionable, using the existing English message style. The helpers add the exception prefix themselves. When replacing an existing error, preserve its substantive explanation and validation behavior unless the task requires a change. When handling a caught error, include its useful explanation and context in the appropriate helper call rather than rethrowing it with stop(e).

For example, a length check following the pattern in R/class_design_optimal.R should include both the actual inputs and their lengths (the call belongs inside the failing validation branch):

stopArgumentLengthOutOfBounds(
    "Must provide exactly one weight in weightsLR per entry of thetaLR.",
    functionName = "getDesignOptimalConditionalError",
    parameter = "weightsLR",
    value = weightsLR,
    constraint = "one weight per thetaLR entry",
    relatedParameter = "thetaLR",
    relatedValue = thetaLR,
    expectedLength = length(thetaLR),
    actualLength = length(weightsLR),
    diagnosticId = "validation.weights_length_matches_effects"
)

The example ID illustrates the naming convention; check existing IDs before assigning one. A choice validation can additionally use context = list(allowedValues = allowedValues), with the actual choices from the validation branch, rather than embedding those choices only in the message.

Review before completing R code changes

  • Inspect the diff for every new or modified error path: verify the helper’s semantics, message, and applicable structured fields.
  • Search for direct calls, for example with rg -n '\b(base::)?stop\s*\(' R -g '*.R', and review matches as code rather than counting documentation or comments. Confirm that the changes introduce no direct stop() calls and that any such calls in the error paths being changed are replaced with the appropriate enriched helpers. The target for the package is exactly one direct call, in .stopWithError().
  • For behavior changes, run relevant tests and verify the error category and metadata where applicable, following the test location rules below. Do not assume metadata will be attached by the default simpleError fallback; inspect metadata through an appropriate configured condition factory when testing it.

Braces in R conditionals

Always use curly braces for every if, else if, and else branch in rpact R code, even when a branch contains only one statement or R would allow the braces to be omitted. This also applies to early returns and conditional expressions used in assignments. Put the branch body on separate lines and indent it with four spaces; write } else { and } else if (...) { on the same line.

For example, do not write:

if (!is.call(call)) return(FALSE)

Write:

if (!is.call(call)) {
    return(FALSE)
}

Apply the same rule to both branches of an if (...) { ... } else { ... } statement. When adding or modifying conditional logic, ensure every branch uses braces; existing unbraced conditionals are not examples to follow.

Braces in R loops

Always use curly braces for every for, while, and repeat loop, even when its body contains only one statement. Put the opening brace on the same line as the loop header, the body on separate lines indented with four spaces, and the closing brace on its own line. Do not use inline loop bodies.

For example:

for (parameter in names(limits)) {
    .assertComparisonLimit(limits[[parameter]], parameter, "summary.TrialComparison")
}

Apply this rule to nested loops as well. Existing unbraced loops are not examples to follow.

R source formatting and syntax

Follow the established style in files such as R/class_core_parameter_set.R, R/class_dictionary.R, R/f_core_utilities.R, and R/f_design_group_sequential.R in the rpact repository:

  • Use four spaces per indentation level, never tabs.
  • Use braced, multiline function bodies, including short functions, S3 generics and methods, R6 methods, and anonymous functions. Put { on the same line as the end of the function signature and } on its own line.
  • Prefer explicit return(value) in named functions and R6 methods that return a value, including early returns. Preserve intentional invisible returns with return(invisible(value)). Do not add artificial return values to functions whose purpose is a side effect.
  • Use <- for assignments and = for named arguments and default argument values. Preserve = where R syntax requires it, such as R6 member lists.
  • Put spaces around assignment, comparison, and binary arithmetic/logical operators and around = in argument lists. Put a space after commas and after control-flow keywords: if (...), for (...), while (...). Write function calls and declarations without a space before (: length(x) and function(x).
  • Do not put spaces just inside parentheses or brackets, or around $, @, ::, or :::. Keep unary operators next to their operand, such as !valid.
  • Write one statement per line; do not join statements with semicolons. Use blank lines between functions and between logical steps within a function. Keep related assignments together.
  • Wrap long signatures and calls at argument boundaries. Indent continuation lines consistently with the surrounding code, and use one argument per line when that makes a long call easier to read. For multiline calls with a separate closing parenthesis, align it with the start of the call. Do not compress nested logic into a long single-line expression.
  • Prefer double-quoted strings; use single quotes when they avoid escaping embedded double quotes. Write TRUE and FALSE, not T and F.
  • Use descriptive camelCase names for variables, arguments, functions, and helpers. Preserve established interfaces and conventions such as S3 method names, class names, C_... constants, and leading dots on internal rpact helpers; do not rename existing interfaces merely for style.

Apply these conventions to new or edited code. Avoid reformatting unrelated legacy code, and preserve evaluation, visibility, and numerical behavior. When reviewing generated code, check loops and function bodies as well as conditionals; syntactically valid one-line forms do not satisfy this style.

Roxygen documentation formatting

When creating or updating Roxygen documentation, use the following source-code format consistently, even when Roxygen could infer sections from their order:

  • Begin and end every documentation block with an empty Roxygen comment line (#'). Keep these separator lines free of trailing whitespace.
  • Separate logical sections with an empty Roxygen comment line, including before @return, @details, @examples, and @export. Keep consecutive @param entries together as one parameter section.
  • Always write an explicit @title tag on its own line, followed by the title on the next Roxygen line. Do not use an untagged first line as an implicit title.
  • Always introduce a description with an explicit @description tag on its own line, followed by the description text on subsequent Roxygen lines. Do not rely on an untagged paragraph being interpreted as the description.
  • Likewise, put section tags such as @details and @examples on their own lines above their content. Keep named tags and short entries such as @param x ..., @rdname ..., and @return ... inline as shown below; @export occupies its own line.
  • Use actual Roxygen syntax in R source: do not add Markdown bold markers to tags or literal HTML entities such as &#x20; to represent blank lines.

For example:

#'
#' @title
#' Access Objects in a Trial Comparison
#'
#' @rdname extract.TrialComparison
#'
#' @description
#' Extracts a contained object by name or position.
#'
#' @param x A `TrialComparison`.
#' @param i A single object name or a positive integer position.
#' @param name An object name, supplied literally after `$`.
#' @param ... Further indices are not supported.
#' @param exact Whether character indices must match exactly, as for list `[[`.
#'   `$` always matches exactly.
#'
#' @return The contained object by reference, or NULL for an unknown name.
#'
#' @details
#' Duplicate names select the first occurrence. Numeric positions refer to the
#' stored object order. R6 members take precedence for `$`: `x$add` is the method
#' even when an object is named "add"; use `x[["add"]]` to select that object.
#' `[[` selects contained objects first and falls back to existing R6 members for
#' other character names. This also preserves existing internal field access.
#' These methods provide extraction; replacing collection entries is not supported.
#' Use [getComparison()] or `$add()` to build or extend the collection.
#'
#' @examples
#' comparison <- getComparison(fixed = getDesignFixed(),
#'     sequential = getDesignGroupSequential(kMax = 2))
#' identical(comparison$fixed, comparison[["fixed"]])
#' identical(comparison[[1]], comparison$fixed)
#'
#' @export
#'

Unit tests and test templates

The rpact-specific rules in this section, including the optional rpact.validator template workflow, apply only to direct development of the rpact package and its tests. When working on another package, such as rpact.code.api or rpact.cloud, create and maintain that package’s tests in its own tests/testthat directory, following its applicable instructions and existing test conventions. Do not create or modify tests for another package in rpact.tests or apply the rpact-specific template rules to those tests. Using rpact as a dependency does not make a package’s tests rpact tests. For tasks spanning multiple packages, apply these rules only to tests of rpact; keep tests of each other package in that package.

All rpact unit tests are hosted and developed in the separate rpact.tests package, except for the small example test test-pkgname.R in the rpact package.

  • Create all new rpact unit tests in rpact.tests/tests/testthat. Do not create new unit tests in the rpact repository.
  • When improving existing tests, check whether they have a corresponding template in rpact.tests/tests-raw/testthat. Update that template as needed to keep the tests and their source templates consistent.
  • Locate the rpact.tests package using the coding agent’s configured projects and workspace folders. It may also be available as a sibling directory of rpact; do not assume a machine-specific absolute path.
  • If rpact.tests cannot be located or accessed, ask the user to provide its local path and make it accessible to the coding agent, for example by adding it to the agent’s workspace. Do not create tests in the rpact repository as a fallback.

Optional template-based regression tests with rpact.validator

When creating general regression tests that freeze the current state of rpact result objects, consider the template-based workflow provided by rpact.validator. Prefer this option for capturing object parameters and calculated results without manually writing repetitive assertions. Handwritten tests remain an option for targeted behavior, edge cases, or checks that are better expressed explicitly.

For template-based tests, create or update the source template in rpact.tests/tests-raw/testthat. Declare the test title with @test_that, create the result object, and pass it to rpact.validator::getUnitTestObject() together with its variable name as a string. For example:

#' @test_that 'getDesignInverseNormal' with default parameters: parameters and results are as expected

design1 <- getDesignInverseNormal()
rpact.validator::getUnitTestObject(design1, "design1")

Rendering the templates generates executable test_that() blocks with expect_equal() assertions for the captured object fields, including expected values, tolerances, and getTestLabel() labels. For this example, these include checks of design1$alphaSpent, design1$criticalValues, and design1$stageLevels. The generated test files belong in rpact.tests/tests/testthat, as required above.

Before rendering, locate and verify both package directories and ensure that rpact.validator is available. Set rpactProjectPath and rpactTestsProjectPath to the resolved local paths of rpact and rpact.tests, respectively; do not hard-code machine-specific paths in shared instructions.

Regeneration must be controlled through the following exact template comment (preserve its spelling, capitalization, and spacing):

#' @exit Do not create the unit tests again

When enforceCreationOfAllUnitTests = FALSE, a template containing this comment is skipped and its unit test file is not regenerated. Always keep enforceCreationOfAllUnitTests = FALSE; never set it to TRUE.

Before every call to rpact.validator::createRpactUnitTests():

  • Identify the specific template whose unit test file is to be generated or regenerated.
  • Check all templates in rpact.tests/tests-raw/testthat. Every template except the selected template must contain the exact @exit comment above. If it is missing, insert it at the beginning of that template before proceeding.
  • Ensure the selected template does not contain the @exit comment; remove it from that template if necessary to enable generation.
  • Run the generator only after these checks and edits are complete, keeping enforceCreationOfAllUnitTests = FALSE.

Render using:

rpact.validator::createRpactUnitTests(
    packageProjectBaseDirectory = rpactProjectPath,
    qualityAssuranceBaseDirectory = rpactTestsProjectPath,
    testFilesProjectBaseDirectory = rpactTestsProjectPath,
    copyUnitTestFilesToTestthatDir = TRUE,
    enforceCreationOfAllUnitTests = FALSE,
    ignoreFilesRegex = NA_character_,
    qaSubDirs = list(
        templates = file.path("tests-raw", "testthat"),
        output = "tests-raw"
    )
)

Treat the templates as the source for generated tests: make changes in the corresponding template and regenerate the test files rather than maintaining changes only in generated output. Review the generated assertions and run the relevant tests. Capturing the current state establishes a regression baseline; it does not independently establish statistical correctness. Do not regenerate expected values merely to make an unexpected regression pass.

New vignettes

  • Create new rpact vignettes as Quarto (.qmd) files in the separate website project rpact-org_website. Do not create new .Rmd vignettes in the rpact package’s vignettes directory.
  • Before creating a vignette, locate rpact-org_website using the coding agent’s configured projects and workspace folders, and verify that its vignettes directory exists and is accessible. Do not assume a machine-specific absolute path.
  • If the website project or its vignettes directory cannot be located or accessed, ask the user to provide the correct path and make it accessible to the coding agent. Do not create the vignette in the rpact repository as a fallback.
  • Choose the appropriate topic directory under rpact-org_website/vignettes: analysis, getting-started, planning, or utilities.
  • Always create a new directory named after the vignette in snake_case within the selected topic directory, and save the vignette as index.qmd inside it. Use this structure: rpact-org_website/vignettes/<topic>/<vignette_name>/index.qmd.
  • Before drafting, read the applicable instructions in the website project and inspect existing vignettes, especially those in the selected topic directory. Follow their layout, overall structure, and writing style, including established conventions for metadata, headings, and code examples.
